title: Food Photography Tips for Bloggers: A Phone-First Setup
summary: Food photography tips for bloggers using a phone: window light, angles by dish, budget styling, a quick edit and the crops Google and Pinterest want.
body_markdown:
Food photography tips for bloggers usually start with gear. They should start with light. A phone beside a window, a sheet of baking paper and a piece of white card will beat a new camera in a dark kitchen every time.


Our point of view: shoot for the crops you need, not for one perfect frame. A recipe page and its Pins need several aspect ratios, so the best photo is one that still works after you crop it four ways. This guide gives you a phone-first setup, step by step.


## Food photography tips for bloggers: what light setup do you need?


Food bloggers need one window, one diffuser and one bounce card. That's the whole kit.


1.


Put your table next to a window so light comes from the side or slightly behind the dish. Light from behind the camera flattens food.


2.


Turn off the room lights. Mixing warm bulbs with daylight gives you color you can't fully fix later.


3.


If sun hits the table directly, hang a sheer curtain or tape baking paper over the window. That softens hard shadows.


4.


Hold or prop a white card, foam board or folded menu on the side opposite the window. It bounces light back into the shadows.


5.


For a moodier look, swap the white card for a black one. Shadows deepen, and dark breads, stews and chocolate look richer.


Shoot at the same time of day for a series. Your recipe archive will look consistent, which matters once your photos sit side by side on a category page.


## What is the best angle for each dish?


The best angle shows the part of the dish that makes people want it. Use the shape of the food to decide.


Dish shape


Examples


Angle


Why


Flat

Overhead

Ramen, curries, pasta, grain bowls


About 45 degrees


Shows depth and the top


Tall


Burgers, layer cakes, stacked pancakes


Straight on


Height is the appeal


Drinks


Smoothies, cocktails, iced coffee


Straight on or slightly above


Shows the glass and the layers


Turn on your phone's grid lines and keep the horizon straight. Don't use digital zoom, which throws away resolution. Step closer instead.


## How do you style food on a budget?


Style with what's already in your kitchen and keep the dish the hero. Food styling tips that cost nothing:


-


Use one or two neutral plates and a matte surface. Shiny surfaces reflect the window.


-


Add a raw ingredient from the recipe next to the plate, such as a halved lemon or a few basil leaves.


-


Wipe the rim of every plate and bowl with a damp paper towel before you shoot.


-


Undercook vegetables slightly for the photo so they stay bright and hold their shape.


-


Add a "human" touch: a spoon mid-scoop, a torn piece of bread, a few crumbs placed on purpose.


Everything in the frame should be something a reader could plausibly have when they cook your recipe. That keeps the photo honest.


## What is a quick editing workflow for food photos?


Edit in this order and stop early. Most food photos need under five minutes.


1.


White balance first, so a white plate looks white.


2.


Exposure, so the brightest part of the food isn't clipped.


3.


A small contrast lift.


4.


A small saturation or vibrance lift, watching that greens don't turn neon.


5.


Crop to your target ratios (next section).


6.


Remove crumbs or smudges you missed, and leave the food itself as you cooked it.

## What photo sizes do recipe cards and Pinterest need?


Recipe pages and Pinterest need different shapes, so plan your crops before you shoot. These are the platform recommendations as of 2026:


Where it shows


Recommended shape


Source

16x9, 4x3 and 1x1, each at least 50,000 pixels (width times height)


[Google recipe structured data guidelines](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/structured-data/recipe)


Pinterest Pin


2:3, such as 1000 x 1500 pixels


[Pinterest product specs](https://help.pinterest.com/en/business/article/pinterest-product-specs)

Pixels are never the problem. Framing is.


If the dish fills the whole horizontal frame, the 1x1 and 2:3 crops cut off the plate. Leave empty space around the food, or shoot one extra frame in portrait for Pinterest.


## How do photos help a recipe rank?


Photos help when Google can understand them. Add the image to your recipe schema, and write alt text that describes the dish, such as "Bowl of red lentil soup topped with yogurt and chili oil." Google's


[image SEO guidelines](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/google-images)


call alt text the most important attribute for image metadata and warn against keyword stuffing.
